Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports business payments to suppliers, vendors, contractors, and other businesses for commercial transactions, procurement, and supply chain payments.
Comments: B2B payments are supported via bank transfers and PesaLink-enabled business payments (e.g., supplier payments, bulk payments). The World Bank PesaLink case study notes bulk payments use-cases, and merchants/PSPs integrate PesaLink for business payments.
revision_notes: Original score (2=Yes) confirmed. Fetched the World Bank Fast Payments Toolkit case study on PesaLink (2021), which lists Business-to-Business as a supported payment/business type on the system, and the iPay Africa merchant page, which describes PesaLink use for paying suppliers, employees and contractors directly from merchant accounts. Both sources support the Value Code unchanged.
revised_comments: PesaLink, Kenya's bank-based instant payment system, supports business-to-business payments. Merchants and payment service providers use it for supplier, contractor and bulk payments, transferring up to KES 999,999 instantly between bank accounts and mobile money wallets, and the World Bank's Fast Payments Toolkit case study on PesaLink recognises business-to-business transfers as a supported use case.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: A consumer protection framework exists for payments/DFS via multiple instruments: Kenya’s Consumer Protection Act (2012) provides general consumer rights, and CBK’s Digital Credit Providers Regulations (2022) include consumer protection requirements (complaints mechanisms, disclosure, debt collection conduct, privacy). This indicates a ‘Yes’ consumer protection framework (even if still evolving for some use-cases like fraud reimbursement).
revision_notes: Original score (3=Yes) confirmed, on stronger evidence than originally cited. The originally cited sources (a KIPPRA blog and a Bowmans note on the Digital Credit Providers Regulations 2022) address fintech and digital lending consumer issues generally rather than a payments-specific framework. Fetched the Central Bank of Kenya's National Payment System (Provision of Electronic Retail Transfers) Regulations, in force per the Kenya Law consolidated revision dated 2022-12-31, which contain a dedicated 'Consumer Protection' section applying specifically to payment service providers: disclosure of fees/terms, mandatory customer care and complaints systems with statutory resolution timelines (30-60 days), and liability rules for unauthorised or defective electronic transfers. This meets the scale's 'Yes' threshold (dedicated payment consumer protection rules). Also found a draft, harmonised Kenya Financial Consumer Protection Framework (Central Bank/CAK, dated March 2026) intended to consolidate currently fragmented sector-specific rules; this is still in draft and does not change the current 'Yes' status, which rests on the existing NPS Regulations.
revised_comments: Kenya's payment service providers are subject to a dedicated consumer protection regime under the Central Bank's National Payment System (Provision of Electronic Retail Transfers) Regulations. These require clear disclosure of fees and terms, a mandatory customer care and complaints-handling system with statutory resolution timelines, and defined liability rules for unauthorised or defective transactions, sitting alongside the general Consumer Protection Act 2012. Kenya's financial regulators are also developing a harmonised Financial Consumer Protection Framework to unify these sector-specific rules.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Kenya’s Data Protection Act 2019 (and implementing regulations) provides mandatory breach notification: data controllers must notify the ODPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a notifiable personal data breach, and data processors must notify controllers within 48 hours.
revision_notes: Original score (3=Mandatory) confirmed. Fetched both cited sources: Bowmans (2024) confirms the Data Protection Act 2019 requires notification of notifiable personal data breaches; CMS Expert Guide (updated October 2025) confirms this applies economy-wide including to payment/financial service providers, with notification to the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner. Consistent with the general 72-hour (controller) / 48-hour (processor) notification timeline. Sources fetched and read; support the Value Code unchanged.
revised_comments: Kenya mandates data breach notification under the Data Protection Act 2019, which applies to payment service providers as data controllers/processors handling transaction data. Data controllers must notify the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner within 72 hours of becoming aware of a notifiable breach, data processors must notify controllers within 48 hours, and affected data subjects must be informed where the breach poses a real risk of harm to their rights and freedoms.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Kenya has general data protection legislation: the Data Protection Act, 2019 applies broadly to personal data processed by payment service providers/fintechs (including financial/transaction data), overseen by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC). No specific payments-only data law provisions were identified beyond the general framework.
revision_notes: Original score (2=General Data Protection Legislation) confirmed. Fetched the DLA Piper Data Protection Laws of the World guide for Kenya (Kenya page last modified 23 March 2026), which confirms the Data Protection Act 2019 remains the primary, general statute covering personal data including that processed by payment providers, with no payments-specific data law identified. Webpinn's guidance on CBK online payment regulation likewise directs payment businesses to comply with the general Data Protection Act rather than a dedicated payments data statute. Sources fetched and read; support the Value Code unchanged.
revised_comments: Kenya's data protection framework rests on the general Data Protection Act, 2019, overseen by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner. It applies broadly to personal data handled by payment service providers and fintechs, including transaction data, but there is no dedicated statute addressing payment data specifically; providers rely on the general Act together with Central Bank data-handling and confidentiality requirements under the National Payment System Regulations.
